http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/saudi.text: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said it was in "deep shock" on Monday, after reporting the deaths of 16 citizens in a sofa factory fire in Saudi Arabia the previous day.Dhaka's Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said that there was "constant communication" with local authorities through the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia."Officials have been instructed to ensure the speedy repatriation of the bodies of the deceased expatriates and to secure all necessary government assistance and compensation for their families," he added.Around seven million Bangladeshis work overseas — the majority in the Middle East.The civil defence agency in the Saudi capital said a fire at an unlicensed facility where furniture was upholstered had been extinguished, without providing details about any casualties."Riyadh civil defence put out a fire at an unlicensed site being used for furniture upholstery," the agency said in a post on X."The necessary regulatory procedures were subsequently completed regarding the site."Like many Gulf nations, Saudi Arabia relies on a vast number of labourers from the subcontinent to help bolster its workforce, especially with jobs involving manual labour.Reports in Saudi media estimate that over three million Bangladeshi nationals reside in the kingdom.Foreign workers in Saudi Arabia do everything from management to cleaning the streets and waiting on tables, in a society where many citizens are reluctant to take jobs they consider menial.

https://www.dw.com/en/putin-denies-fresh.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KofK Putin said he was grateful to countries which were making an effort to mediate a resolution to the conflict Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Russia is not preparing to mobilize more men to fight, President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, describing such speculation as Ukrainian "disinformation." In 2022 and a few months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin ordered the unpopular "partial mobilization" of reservists amid a string of military set backs. The decision prompted an exodus of draft-age men from Russia and the Kremlin has since repeatedly denied plans for another mobilization. "There is no scenario today that would require mobilization," Putin told a plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok. "This is a disinformation campaign by the enemy in the run-up to the State Duma elections, aimed at influencing the outcome," he added, referring to Russian parliamentary elections later this month. "As is well known, our people enlist voluntarily and sign a contract." Putin had already dismissed mobilization speculations earlier this week, calling such reports "utter nonsense" and an "information attack" against Russia. What did Putin say about peace in Ukraine? Putin once again claimed there was a chance for peace with Ukraine , but stressed the conflict must be resolved by Moscow and Kyiv. His statements come amid intensified Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital. Meanwhile, Kyiv has intensified its attacks deeper within Russia , striking online retailers and other civilian targets. Russia launches missile and drone barrage on Kyiv To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Putin thanked countries which were making an effort to mediate a resolution to the conflict. He said the US and China, among others, were ready to support a peace settlement. "Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved ​by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine. ⁠This ​is the correct ​approach. Yet, we are grateful ​to everyone attempting to ‌ contribute to a settlement. Is there ​a ⁠chance? In my view, yes, there is," Putin said. Still, he went on to condemn Ukraine, saying warnings about risks to planes in Russian airspace amount to "state terrorism." On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that his country's drones have made Russian airspace unsafe for planes. Putin was speaking during the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP How has Moscow responded to Zelenskyy's airspace warning? On Thursday, Russia's Transport Ministry said it has provided clarifications to foreign airlines about Russian airports' and airspace safety measures. "They work very closely with us and ​understand all our rules, standards and how we ​ensure flight safety," Russian news agency Interfax ​quoted ‌Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin as saying. He added that the clarifications were given in response to requests from foreign carriers. On Wednesday, Russian aviation watchdog Rosaviatsiya stressed in a statement that the country's "air transport, its ground infrastructure, continue to operate ​normally, receiving and dispatching flights, including those of foreign airlines." European and US carriers have avoided Russian airspace since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, other airlines from China, Turkey and the Gulf states still use it. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Australia’s immediate neighbours are trusted more than historic allies, according to a new survey AAP reports on, which shows the United States is increasingly considered a “threat”. Only half of the Australians polled in a YouGov survey, commissioned by the Australia Institute, considered longtime ally the US a “friend”. Meanwhile 42% perceived America as a “threat” (defined as a nation viewed with caution or suspicion). Only 4% of young voters labelled the US a “close friend” while over half of young Australians considered it a threat. Two-thirds of One Nation voters perceive the US as a friend, with the Coalition close behind. Labor voters are largely split and only one-quarter of Greens voters view the global superpower positively. Only 21% of respondents had confidence in Donald Trump to “do the right thing” in world affairs, ahead of only the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un. https://www.businessinsider.com/nato-lat.text: NATO member Latvia is building a wall of automated anti-drone defenses along its border with Russia, with human soldiers responsible only for deciding when and whether to fire. It aims to detect and neutralize "any drone which flies in," defense minister Raivis Melnis told Business Insider. And the goal, he explained, is to "build an autonomous system" that leverages the technology to "reduce the number of soldiers" required "to operate those systems." "The only thing which will be left for the soldier is the final decision to neutralize," he said. "Otherwise, detection, tracking, and launching, that's autonomous." Latvia's decision comes as automation is becoming increasingly common in weaponry and defense tech, including in Ukraine, where technology has advanced to enable AI and computer vision to find targets, fly drones, and drive robots even when connectivity with an operator is lost. Latvia wants this kind of autonomy across its new network of radars, sensors, command-and-control systems, and interceptor drones. As a neighboring country, Latvia is particularly concerned about the possibility of Russian aggression. It has reported multiple drone incursions. These have included drones that it said were Russian or that had entered its airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare. Latvia, a country of fewer than 2 million people, sees automation as a way to boost its combat power without more troops. Ukraine has made the same calculation, using increasingly autonomous weapons to help offset Russia's larger military. Agris Kipurs, CEO of Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics, previously told Business Insider that the smaller, front-line NATO nations need systems that let fewer operators do more. "And pretty much the only answer to that is autonomy," he said. The company makes drones used by Ukraine's military. It also makes an AI-enabled drone interceptor called Blaze that has been bought by multiple NATO militaries. Latvia's new defensive project is directly inspired by Ukraine, which has developed cheap weaponry like interceptor drones to combat Russia's attacks. Latvia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters and one of the militaries most keenly adopting battlefield lessons from its fight. Melnis said that interceptor drones have proved to have a "really high reliability and kill ratio in Ukraine, where the Ukrainians are fighting" one-way attack drone bombardments. Ukraine is increasingly relying on autonomy to allow systems to decrease the cognitive load on soldiers while strengthening the defense overall. Automating processes reduces the demand for human input, though they remain important for engagement and kill decisions. Tech used on the battlefield is becoming increasingly autonomous; however, there are still limits to how much they can act beyond human control. Ukraine says that it will also keep humans involved on principle, giving them the final decision whether to engage. Latvia, Ukraine, and other allies want to use these kinds of anti-drone defenses because they're so much cheaper than traditional, expensive methods like missiles. Those defenses are not sustainable as the only solution against the masses of cheap drones. Melnis said that it's key to have a "cheap but reliable system" to stop drones. Latvia is using "modern technology and a cheap technology in comparison with a missile," he said. Allies are buying and developing these cheaper anti-drone systems. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in June that "long-term we cannot continue by shooting down drones with very costly interceptors, so we have to find interception techniques which are of the same costs as the drones." Latvia and other NATO allies have used fighter jets like F-35s, F-16s, and Rafales to shoot down drones entering their airspace with expensive air-to-air missiles. Melnis said the new system is designed to make jets a backup, serving only as "the secondary means" of stopping any drone that penetrates the wall. Melnis said the anti-drone wall is important for more than just his country's defense. The "border is not a Russian-Latvian border," he said. "It is a Russia-NATO, Russia-Europe border." He said that while this stretch of border is between Russia and Latvia, "we are NATO, and we are a European Union country." Any drone that crosses the border, he said, "that's the drone coming into NATO airspace. That's the drone coming into Europe."
